title: Of presumption
hookLine: he describes his own faults with honesty and humor (Essays 2.17)

cards: I work too hard. I care too much. I'm a perfectionist.

Ask someone to name their flaws, and sometimes this is what comes back: a boast wearing a disguise. Montaigne answers the question for real, in an essay he calls Of Presumption, and he doesn't disguise a thing.
He goes through his faults the way you'd go through a junk drawer, holding each one up to the light, and some of them are funny.

teach.h: TOO HIGH ON SELF, TOO LOW ON OTHERS.
teach.b: First, what presumption is. Montaigne says it has two sides: thinking too highly of ourselves, and thinking too little of others.
His own lean, he says, runs the other way: he tends to prize what others have and undervalue what's his. Second, the list. He's shorter than average, he says, and counts it a real drawback.
His body was strong but clumsy at the skills a gentleman was supposed to have: dancing, tennis, wrestling, he was no good at them.
His hands were so awkward that he couldn't read his own handwriting. He couldn't properly fold a letter, carve meat at the table, or saddle a horse. No excuses come attached.

teach.h: PROUD OF WHAT EVERYONE THINKS THEY HAVE.
teach.b: Third, the one thing he's proud of. Is there anything he does prize in himself? Yes: his judgment, his good sense.
Then the joke lands on him. That's the one quality, he points out, that nobody in the world thinks they're short of. So even his pride is ordinary.
Fourth, plainly, with a smile. This isn't self-hatred. He isn't groveling for reassurance, and he isn't fishing for compliments.
He's accurate, and he's amused, describing his own faults the way he'd describe the weather.
My faults, plainly, sounds like I'm bad with dates instead of I'm a terrible friend: true, specific, survivable, and maybe a little funny.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Presumption as a model for honest self-description: naming faults plainly, neither boasting nor groveling, and keeping a sense of humor.

o: a lawyer's guess about guilt before any proof is given
thinking too highly of ourselves and too little of others
boldly expecting others to do us favors without asking

p: too high on self, too low on others
the quality nobody thinks they lack

s: he lists real ones: short height, clumsy hands, handwriting he couldn't read, no skill at dancing or tennis.
he says he couldn't read his own handwriting
his hands, he says, were that awkward.
the one quality he prizes is one he says everyone thinks they have
his good sense; nobody, he points out, thinks they're short of it.

games.q: you're writing a book about yourself that strangers will read. you've reached the part about your shortcomings. what does Montaigne do?
o: skip it and list his achievements.
list them plainly: short height, clumsy hands, handwriting he can't read.
write that his only fault is working too hard.
games.why: he lists real faults, specific and a little funny, and then turns the joke on his one point of pride: good sense, which nobody thinks they lack.

practice: Choose one ordinary fault of yours, not the worst thing about you, and say it to yourself in one plain sentence, the way Montaigne would, with no excuse at the front and no attack at the end: I lose my keys, I interrupt when I'm excited, I put things off.
Hold that sentence for a while. If something about it is a little funny, let it be funny.

wordCard.voice: Of presumption. Montaigne's essay on thinking too much of ourselves, in which he lists his own faults, clumsy hands and all, honestly and with a smile. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: my faults, plainly. No speech for the defense, and none for the prosecution. See you tomorrow.
